1:
Who the besieger was, and what the thirty-two kings amounted to, is settled first. Gill makes him the second of the name, son of the king whom Asa once hired against Baasha. Clarke adds that several manuscripts and early editions read Ben-hadar instead, as the Greek does, and leaves open whether this is Asa's man, his son or his grandson. Ellicott treats the name as the inherited title of the Syrian kings, and infers from a later verse that this one's father had beaten Omri. On the confederacy they agree: Clarke calls the thirty-two tributary chieftains of Syria and the neighbouring country, where once every town had its own ruler, and Ellicott describes small kingdoms federated under a leading power, which in David's day was Zobah and is now Damascus. Henry asks what the quarrel was about and finds no answer in the text, covetousness and ambition never wanting a pretence. His own explanation is Israel's apostasy, which has made formidable again a people David had subdued; Asa's hiring of these Syrians shows how dearly posterity may pay for bringing in a foreign force.

The first demand and the answer to it are read as a transfer of sovereignty. Keil and Delitzsch set out the two messages plainly and call the reply pusillanimous. Ellicott is more precise: the demand asserts and the answer accepts a Syrian overlordship, in which the vassal's goods and family are acknowledged to belong to his superior. His further point is that the surrender was not at discretion: it was Ben-hadad who refused all qualified submission. Gill notes that the claim was made as of possession, not of right, Ahab being in no condition to resist. Clarke supposes the humiliation was calculated, to soften a barbarous enemy and perhaps secure better terms. Henry sees the effect of sin instead, since a king who had provoked God to depart from him had no protection left. His sharpest stroke is that the silver and gold had already been prepared for Baal, so that losing them was a forfeiture; guilt, he adds, dispirits men and makes them cowards.

What the second demand added to the first is a real puzzle. Clarke says it is not easy to see the difference, since the silver, the gold, the wives and the children were already the most desirable things the king had. He reports Jarchi's conjecture that the book of the law was what Ben-hadad meant to carry off, and concludes for himself that the whole city was to be sacked and given over to the soldiers. Ellicott reaches the same end another way, that a demand amounting to the plunder of Samaria neither expects nor wants acceptance, and is a refusal of anything short of unconditional surrender. Gill observes only that a day's grace was allowed for the answer. Henry divides the insolence into three: a covetousness not content to call the goods his without handling them, a spite that sends servants to rifle a palace and take whatever the owner is known to be fond of, and an injustice that extends one man's surrender to all his subjects.

The appeal to the elders is where the chapter turns. Ellicott notes that Ahab falls back on an exceptional appeal to the patriotism of his people. He identifies them as the northern representatives of the senate that had existed since Moses, a body with power of concurrence and not of advice only, though liable to be overborne by the royal power. Henry watches the two spirits change places. The king speaks poorly, asking his council whether the enemy is not plainly seeking mischief, while they answer bravely and promise to stand by a refusal. The refusal is modestly worded, owning the overlordship and standing by the first surrender while declining the second, and Henry doubts it would have been made at all had the people not animated him.
7:
The council is the one piece of good management the commentators allow the king. Gill says his sneaking spirit was a little roused by the second message, and calls the summoning of the elders wisdom in him. Clarke explains why their answer was unanimous and firm: the elders had everything at stake, and preferred a desperate defence to a tame surrender on degrading and ruinous terms. Gill will not let the refusal itself pass for courage, since even with the council behind him the king delivered it in a poor sneaking manner. Keil and Delitzsch give the wording without comment on the spirit of it, that what was asked at the first would be done but this thing could not be, and treat what followed as an attempt to overawe a weak-minded man by threats.

The boast about the dust of Samaria is read two ways. Clarke reports the Chaldee paraphrase, which makes it a claim about numbers: the dust of the city would not be enough for the soles of the feet of the army he was bringing, so that there would scarcely be room for them to stand. Ellicott hears a threat as well as a boast, since dust is what a city becomes when it is razed. He adds the explanation Josephus gives, that if every Syrian took a single handful they could raise a mound higher than the walls. His portrait of the besieger comes from the same source, a luxurious braggart who receives the reply at a feast, drinks himself drunk, and will not bestir himself but orders the assault in one haughty word, which may mean array the troops or place the engines.

The answer to it is the line the chapter is remembered for. Gill's whole note is that it was very mildly and very wisely said. Keil and Delitzsch render the proverb as a warning that the man girding himself should not boast like the man loosening his girdle, and match it with the Latin saying against singing a triumph before the victory. Clarke agrees that the words were proverbial and gives the Chaldee expansion, that a man who girds himself and goes down to the battle should not boast like one who has conquered and come home from it.
12:
The attack is ordered from a drinking booth, and the commentators make much of that. Gill notes the hour, since noon or earlier shows what these men were addicted to. Keil and Delitzsch describe the booths themselves, made of branches and shrubs, such as are still put up in the East for kings and generals instead of tents. Clarke derives the English word for them from the butterfly, because a tent spread out resembled one in shape and in painting, and takes the single word of command for a military term meaning begin the attack. Henry draws the moral: had the man not been secure he would not have sat down to drink, and had he not been drunk he would not have been so secure. His comparison is Belshazzar, and his question is how a commander could prosper who preferred his pleasure to his business and kept his thirty-two allies drinking when they should have been at their posts.

Who the prophet was nobody can say, and the guesses are worth more than the answer. Gill reports the Jewish writers' identification with Micaiah the son of Imlah, perhaps one of the men Obadiah had hidden in the cave. Clarke repeats that guess and then makes a bolder one, that it is strange we hear nothing of Elijah or Elisha here, and asks whether this may not be one of them in disguise. Ellicott takes the anonymity as a fact about the period rather than a puzzle: the schools of the prophets were forming again now that the enmity of the court had ended at Carmel, and Elijah is absent from these political errands because he reserved himself for a higher mission. His further observation is that the king receives the message with perfect confidence, having returned in profession to an allegiance he may never have wholly given up. Henry wonders instead that any prophet was sent to such a man, and answers that it was for the people's sake, to magnify a mercy that would either bring him to repentance or leave him inexcusable, and to humble the besieger's pride first.

The two hundred and thirty-two are identified three ways. Clarke makes them the royal bodyguard, the king's own regiment in Samaria, which is why the prophet orders him to put himself at their head. Ellicott makes them the armour-bearers of the territorial chiefs, picked men and well armed. Henry makes them pages, few in number and unacquainted with war, which is the point of choosing them. On the seven thousand behind them Clarke exclaims at how low Israel had fallen, and passes on the notion that these were the seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal; Ellicott reckons them a garrison able to man the walls and unfit to take the field. Gill's comment is that so small a number of raw young men against such an army is the wonder of the thing.

The sortie was made at noon, and the hour was chosen. Ellicott takes from Josephus the reason, that the besiegers were resting unarmed in the heat of the day. Gill has the men go out openly and with courage, and observes that the account does not say their king went at their head, which he thinks it would have said. Keil and Delitzsch record the order that met them, that in his drunken arrogance the besieger had them taken alive whether they came for peace or for war. Henry turns that order into the hinge of the battle, since killing them would have been easier and safer, and the attempt to seize them gave them the chance to kill the men sent to do it. His summary is that a drunkard forgets the law, and that this one forgot both the policy and the justice of war in one command.
17:
The order to take the sallying party alive is given two motives. Clarke makes it confidence with a practical edge, that men brought in rather than killed might furnish useful information. Keil and Delitzsch let the wording carry the whole weight, since the command is repeated for both cases, whether the men came to treat or to fight, and so takes no account of what they might actually be doing. Gill notes the marching order, that the young men went out ahead of the seven thousand, and reads the first clause of the command as providing for an embassy, men coming out to propose terms.

How the rout happened is the one place in the chapter where a commentator declines a miracle. Ellicott compares the attack of this handful, backed by a sally of the whole garrison, with the slaughter of the Philistine host in the days of Saul and with Gideon's night attack on Midian. He thinks Israelites probably rose from various lurking-places to join the pursuit, and says plainly that the event need not be supposed miraculous, since the sudden dispersion of vast Oriental armies is not uncommon in history. The lesson he draws is Jonathan's, that there is no restraint upon the Lord to save by many or by few. Gill keeps the arithmetic that makes it marvellous, reckoning the slain at the exact number of the men who went out against them, and allows that what they met may have been a detachment rather than the whole Syrian army. Clarke's whole account of the collapse is that the Syrians were doubtless panic-struck.

The pursuit is where the king finally appears. Keil and Delitzsch have the governors' servants in front and the army behind, each man killing his man, after which the Aramaeans broke and their king got away on horseback with some of his cavalry. Gill explains the king of Israel's late entrance, that he came out when he saw the enemy fleeing and his own men pursuing, perhaps with fresh troops who were now willing enough to join him; he cites Josephus for a second army kept inside the walls. Keil and Delitzsch close the episode with the horses and chariots cut up and a great slaughter made of the Syrians.
22:
The warning comes before the danger, and Henry makes the timing the point. He observes that the king was now secure and looking only a little way ahead, as men careless of their souls are commonly careless of their affairs. The prophet, who had been let into the counsels of the enemy, told him the attempt would be renewed at the turn of the year, by men bent on retrieving their honour. Henry's inference is that the decree of the end did not excuse the use of means, and that a man who will not strengthen himself when told to tempts God rather than trusts him. Ellicott fixes the season, the early part of the next year once winter was over, the time when kings go out to battle, and Gill notes that the messenger was the same prophet as before. Henry's wonder at the whole episode is that an idolater and a persecutor should be a conqueror, which he refers to the wise and holy ends God has in letting wicked men prosper.

The Syrian explanation of the defeat is theological, and all four treat it as such. Keil and Delitzsch set out the two causes the ministers named, the supposed nature of Israel's gods and the standing of the vassal-kings, and note that both were things that could be altered. Clarke supplies the military fact underneath the theology, that a small army had used the heights and broken ground where cavalry and chariots were nearly useless, and would have no such advantage in the plain. Ellicott develops the belief itself: tutelary gods are natural to a polytheism that limits each god by multiplying them, and most of the land where Jehovah was worshipped was hill-country, with Samaria in the mountains of Ephraim. He adds that Israel's armies were infantry with almost no cavalry, and fought on hills by preference, as Barak did on Tabor and Saul on Gilboa, and that worship in the high places may have helped the mistake along. Henry itemises the errors as a catechist would, that they made Jehovah many when he is one, a local deity of one nation when he is the ruler of all the world, and a god of the hills because their prophet had spoken of lifting his eyes to the hills and of a holy mountain.

The second piece of advice was administrative. Clarke says the vassal-kings were either unacquainted with military affairs or without competent skill, and that experienced captains were to replace them. Henry sharpens the contrast into commanders by birth against commanders by merit, men inured to war who would not affect a show but would go through with the business. His rule from it is that every man should be employed in what he was brought up to and preferred to what he is fit for. Ellicott sees policy under the superstition here too, since organising the tributary kings' troops under the overlord's own officers increased the central power. Gill and Henry both remark what the proposal assumed about Syrian resources, that a country could replace horse for horse and chariot for chariot after so great a defeat.

Henry's note runs on from here into the next engagement, and two of its observations belong to the ground rather than the argument. He places the Syrian camp near Aphek in the tribe of Asher, and supposes the city had been among his father's conquests, with the flat country about it suiting his purpose exactly. His description of the two armies is the chapter's most quoted sentence, the children of Israel in their two battalions looking like two little flocks of kids, small in number and mean in equipage, while the Syrians filled the country with their noise and baggage. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the bare sequence, that with the new year the muster was made and the march to Aphek followed.
26:
Where the second battle was fought is not settled, and the numbers on the Israelite side are read as evidence. Clarke places this Aphek in Libanus, on the river Adonis between Heliopolis and Biblos, while granting that several towns bore the name. Ellicott takes the name for the common word meaning a fortress and offers two candidates that suit a plain between Israel and Syria, the Aphek of the Philistine muster in the plain of Esdraelon and a place about six miles east of the Sea of Galilee. Gill counts the Israelite force as unchanged from the year before, the two hundred and thirty-two and the seven thousand, with not a man missing. Ellicott prefers the marginal rendering that they were victualled or supplied rather than all present, and draws an inference from the smallness of the force: an army no larger than this a year after so great a victory suggests that defeats before the siege of Samaria had already broken the strength of Israel. Keil and Delitzsch supply the picture the verse gives, two little flocks of goats cut off from the herd, encamped probably on the mountain slopes by the plain of Jezreel.

The reason given for the promised victory is the Syrian boast, and it draws out the chapter's widest comment. Keil and Delitzsch state it plainly: because the Syrians had called Jehovah a mountain-god and not a god of the valleys, the multitude would be given into Israel's hand. Clarke reads it as God resenting a blasphemy and determining to punish it, so that the defeat should show his power to be everywhere and the multitude of a host nothing against him. Ellicott thinks this messenger is not the man who came before, since by the evidence of a later verse the prophetic order was numerous by now. His larger point is that the majesty of God is here vindicated before the Syrians as much as before Israel, as it was later against the blasphemy of Sennacherib, and that this answers to Solomon's prayer that all the peoples of the earth might know God's name. He treats it as a foreshadowing of the view, worked out fully in the prophets, that all nations have some knowledge of God and stand on probation before him, and adds that the monotheism of Israel can hardly have been without influence on its neighbours while the memory of Solomon's empire lasted.

The battle, when it came, was delayed and then decisive. Gill explains the week of waiting by position, the Israelites holding a hill and the Syrians unwilling to attack them there for the very reason they had given for changing ground. Keil and Delitzsch report the slaughter of a hundred thousand in one day and the flight of the remainder into the city, where the wall fell on twenty-seven thousand; they suppose the fugitives had climbed the wall to make a stand on it. On that wall the explanations divide. Clarke's first thought is that the Israelites sapped it so that a large portion fell and buried the men, and his second is that the hand of God was more immediately in it, probably by a burning wind. Ellicott keeps to the city wall falling either by earthquake or in the storming, and treats the figures as he treats other large numbers in the book, possibly corrupt though the ancient versions agree, and otherwise well illustrated by the slaughter that follows when Eastern armies are massed in a small space. Gill adds that Aphek was probably already in Syrian hands and meant for a retreat, and Clarke that the city was now effectually taken, its king hidden in an inner chamber with the servants he was about to take counsel with.
31:
The surrender is staged, and its dress is explained from one famous parallel. Gill sets out the trap: going out meant falling into Israelite hands, staying meant a city whose wall had fallen, and the inner chamber could not hide a man long. Clarke and Ellicott both compare the sackcloth and ropes with the burghers of Calais surrendering to Edward III, men offering themselves as helpless criminals to sue for mercy. Gill reads the ropes as a token brought along to say that hanging was deserved, and that the king might do with them as seemed good to him. Henry explains why they expected better, since the kings of Israel had a reputation for clemency beyond their neighbours, their government being, as governments then went, one of the gentlest. His conjecture is that the reputation came from the God of Israel, whose name was proclaimed gracious and merciful, his kings being assumed to follow the pattern.

The reversal between the chapter's opening and this scene is what the commentators dwell on. Clarke marks the vicissitude: the man lately the haughtiest of tyrants, whom Ahab had addressed as his lord, would now be glad to pass for Ahab's slave. Henry divides the embassy's business in two, to present their master as a penitent and as a beggar for his life. On the penitence he is unsparing, since many who pretend to repent of a wrong-doing that has failed would have justified and gloried in it had it prospered. On the beggary he sets the two tempers side by side, the hectoring and swearing of the first verses against the crouching and whining of these, and draws the rule that the most haughty in prosperity are commonly the most abject in adversity, an even spirit being the same in both.

The word that saved the embassy was caught as an omen. Gill says they watched the king's words and bearing as closely as a soothsayer watches for a lucky sign, and notes that the verb is sometimes used of divining. Ellicott reports that the clause has been much discussed and emendations proposed, but thinks the received rendering accurate, and that the Greek translators understood the watching as augury. His reading of the exchange is graphic and turns on the titles: the Syrians say thy slave, the king of Israel says my brother, and the envoys snatch up a word which by Eastern custom was a pledge of amity that could not be recalled. Keil and Delitzsch say the same more shortly, that the words were laid hold of as a good omen, and both note that the pledge was sealed publicly when the beaten king was taken into the chariot.

Who speaks the terms is disputed, and what they amount to is disputed too. Gill observes that the name is absent from the original of the verse and prefers to give the whole offer to Ahab, whose superabundant kindness, conqueror though he was, went so far as to propose it himself. Keil and Delitzsch keep the usual attribution, a beaten king promising to restore his father's conquests and to grant quarters in his own capital so as to keep the victor in this favourable mood. Clarke explains the privilege from commercial practice, that foreigners were assigned a place to deposit and sell their goods, and follows it into the origin of European settlements in Asia, where an inch given became an ell taken and the guests ended by giving laws to their hosts. Ellicott renders the word as squares or quarters and presses what the grant implies, since a right to quarters for residence, trade, perhaps garrison, in a king's capital belongs only to a sovereign over him. His judgement on the whole transaction is that it was made hastily and on insufficient security, and that a war conducted under prophetic guidance should not have been ended without prophetic sanction.
35:
The messenger is identified by tradition and the body he came from is explained at length. Gill reports that the Jews and Josephus make him Micaiah, thinks it probable, and notes that the king recognised him once the disguise came off. Ellicott repeats the identification and observes that it agrees with the narrative two chapters later. His longer note is on the phrase itself, which appears here for the first time though the thing is as old as Samuel and his company of disciples. Since the prophetic office was never hereditary as the priesthood and the kingship were, he takes sonship to mean discipleship, and the schools to have been places of higher religious education attended by many who never looked for the vocation. His conjecture is that the institution had lapsed and was revived to secure the victory just won over the worship of Baal, and he contrasts the awe with which these men regarded Elijah with the affectionate trust they showed Elisha. Keil and Delitzsch explain the commission rather than the man, a disciple instructed to convey the sentence by a symbolic action, as Nathan had done with David, so that the king should pronounce it on himself.

The refusal and its punishment are defended as proportionate. Clarke reads the opening words as meaning that God had commanded the blow, so that refusing it forfeited the refuser's life. He adds the emblem the whole scene was to carry, that as this man died for not smiting when God required it, so the king had forfeited his life for not smiting the enemy God had put in his hands. He grants that the lion looks like hard measure and answers that the man was himself one of the sons of the prophets, knew that God often delivered his counsels in this way, and could do no injury by a blow which the man struck asked for. Gill reaches the same verdict, that a prophet who disregarded what another prophet said in God's name was inexcusable. Ellicott simply refers to the earlier instance in the book where a lion executed a sentence of the same kind. Gill's observation on the second man is the sharpest thing in the passage: he is not called a neighbour, nor a son of the prophets, but a plain countryman, and so made no difficulty about taking the request at its word.

The disguise is a textual question on which all three agree against the version. Keil and Delitzsch say the word does not mean ashes at all but answers to the Chaldee term for a head-band, and have the man bind his eyes before taking his place in the king's path. Clarke argues the point out, that it is not clear how ashes on the face could disguise anybody, that Houbigant would read bandage instead, and that the two words differ only by the corner of a letter where one is square and the other round. His evidence is the Greek, which has him bind his eyes with a fillet, and the Chaldee, which covers them with a cloth; he admits that the collated manuscripts offer no variant and still thinks bandage certainly right. Ellicott agrees that it should be a bandage over the head, covering the face, and says why: the man was to look like a wounded soldier. His remaining difficulty is the wound itself, since unless it carried some symbolic application to the king or to Israel he cannot see what purpose it served.
39:
The tale told by the roadside is a trap of the same make as Nathan's. Keil and Delitzsch call it a fictitious story, a soldier given a prisoner to keep on pain of his own life or a talent of silver. Clarke says the drift is obvious to a reader and was not obvious to the king, who was led by it to pass sentence on himself. Ellicott groups it with Nathan's parable and with the similar plea used on David afterwards, as a device for making a man condemn himself, and observes that here it drew out no compunction but only the sullen displeasure that appears again in the next chapter. Gill supplies the staging, a loud cry from the roadside to make the king stop, and a plea of being busy here and there while the prisoner slipped away.

The unmasking turns the sentence round. Gill has the man strip off the linen cloth and speak not his own sense but in the name of the Lord, for which he had authority, so that the words should carry the more weight. Clarke adds a practical note on the cloth, that it was light enough to see through and still served for a disguise. Keil and Delitzsch render the charge as the letting go of the man of God's ban, and Ellicott prefers a man under my curse. Ellicott's account of the fault is the fullest in the chapter: the rashness may have come partly of compassion and partly of weakness, as Saul's disobedience did, and in neither case had it any right to stand between God's judgment and the man it was pronounced upon. His rule from it is that even soft-heartedness, as in the case of Eli, may be treason to the cause of righteousness. He hears the prophet speaking at once as a patriot, jealous with what proved a sagacious jealousy of a lenity that left Israel's deadly enemy unsubdued, and as the representative of a judgment the king had treated as of no account. Clarke notes where the sentence was executed, at Ramoth-gilead.

The king's way of taking it is read as the chapter's last fault. Keil and Delitzsch say only that he went home sullen and morose to Samaria. Clarke distinguishes the two words, heavy at the tidings and displeased with the prophet who brought them, and then makes the observation the whole episode turns on: had the displeasure been with himself, and had he humbled his soul before God, even judgments so circumstantially foretold might have been averted.

Clarke's note on this last verse runs on into two long excursions, and both are worth recording. The first reopens the twenty-seven thousand killed at Aphek, on the ground that the rendering of the word for wall is doubtful. He reports Kennicott's observation that the same consonants without one letter give the word for heat, used of the sun, of vehement heat, and of a wind named from its parching quality, which Castel explains by burning, rage and poison. The instances he musters are the east wind that carries a man away in Job, rendered burning in the Greek, the east wind that dried the fruit in Ezekiel, the wind of the Lord in Hosea, and the blasting of Amos, which the Latin and Syriac both make a hot wind. His conclusion is that the men died not under masonry but under a scorching wind. His second excursion is the one he had promised earlier, the burghers of Calais who surrendered to Edward III in sackcloth and halters, and he turns their leader and his five companions into a portrait of genuine patriotism, a thing he reckons almost as rare as the phoenix and widely different from the spurious kind that cries up its country while it has nothing in view but places, pensions and profits.
